segments.en: Good to be with you, I'm Tony Dokoupil.
The breaking news, right now.
State of emergency-- millions along the Atlantic Coast from the Carolinas to Maine now in the path of a nor'easter.
The monster storm expected to bring up to a half foot of rain, 60-mile-an-hour winds, and, for some, nearly 20 foot waves.
Also tonight, Hurricane Nolo targeting Hawaii, the third hurricane to hit the island since August.
Our Rob Marciano tracking it all.
CBS News exclusive-- the president of Iran, what he told our Margaret Brennan tonight about his new proposal to end the war.
[DOLLY PARTON, "9 TO 5"] Working 9 to 5.
TONY DOKOUPIL: Celebrating Dolly Parton, 9-2-5.
And Steve Hartman on the road with a double dose of inspiration.
DR.
JASPER: All of this stuff that we went through, all of the negative days, made us who we are now.
NARRATOR: From CBS News headquarters in New York, this is the CBS Evening News with Tony Dokoupil.

And good evening, it's great to have you with us on a Friday night, but ahead of what forecasters say could be a dangerous weekend for more than 60 million people along the East Coast, we've been hearing the warnings.
Now you're going to see the winds already churning up surf, but this is nothing, we're told, compared to what's coming.
An old fashioned nor'easter gathering strength as it moves up the coast, canceling concerts and baseball games, and prompting the governors of New York and New Jersey to declare states of emergency.
The fear is flooding along the coast and power outages across parts of New England.
We've got team coverage on this, starting with Lilia Luciano.
She's in Sea Bright, New Jersey for us.
Lilia, what do you see?
What can you tell us?
Well, Tony, we've already seen conditions escalate over the last several hours, and it hasn't even started raining.
There's a flood and a high wind warning through the weekend.
Folks here and all along the coast are bracing for the worst, and they have seen it.
This area was devastated during Superstorm Sandy.
Towns along the New Jersey shore are getting battered by coastal flooding.
In Ship Bottom, roads are submerged.
Some drivers attempted to push through the rising floodwaters, while some residents are grabbing what little they can and fleeing to higher ground on foot.
In Sea Bright homeowners and businesses are preparing for the worst, but bar owner Michael Cardelefe says his doors will stay open.
You stay open during the storm?
We'll stay open as-- we're like the local watering hub.
And Donovan's reef is the kind of place where, when we have a storm, we get busier.
LILIA LUCIANO: The powerful nor'easter is threatening to pack winds over 60 miles per hour, waves of up to 11 feet.
The system is already kicking up high surf and causing beach erosion in Ocean City, New Jersey, where block after block is underwater.
On New York's Long Island, where a state of emergency has been declared, crews built a wall of sand along the beach to keep rising tide away from homes.
ROBERT KENNEDY: If the tide goes out, we don't expect to have such bad flooding.
If the tide stays in, it could increase the flooding in the village.
LILIA LUCIANO: In Plymouth, Massachusetts, boaters are clearing out the harbor.
Just want people to take some extra precaution, plan ahead a little bit.
LILIA LUCIANO: My colleague, Tom Hanson, is in Cohasset, Massachusetts, which sits right in the bull's eye of the storm.
Well, as you can see, the waves have begun lashing this coastline as this monster storm slowly turns toward our direction.
Even though we are 300 miles away, we have begun to feel the impacts.

Now, much of this coastline is protected by seawalls, but a lot of those seawalls are under repair, which has officials concerned because that sustained wind is expected to push ocean water over the seawalls.
And we could see up to 3 feet of coastal flooding.
Now, if that's not enough, this storm is also expected to dump half a foot of rain, prompting officials to warn residents to avoid low-lying and coastal areas.
And I spoke with the mayor of Sea Bright.
He was telling me that he was told the flooding could reach seven feet, that they expect they could lose power, and that certainly some residents will lose their cars.
Although there are no mandatory evacuations in place, he is urging residents in low-lying areas or in first floors to seriously consider relocating.
Tony.
You can understand why.
Lilia, thank you.
Let's turn now to meteorologist Rob Marciano, got our forecast tracking the nor'easter along with Hurricane Nolo headed for Hawaii.
Rob, what can we expect?
Well, the mid-Atlantic has been dealing with this one for days now, Tony.
And now the conditions will only deteriorate as we go through the weekend here in the Northeast.
The advisories have expanded throughout the day today.
And Philadelphia under a wind advisory, all of New Jersey and along the coastline, especially the extreme eastern New England.
Providence, Boston, high wind warning is up.
And those coastal flood alerts-- several high tide cycles ago.
If you live in one of those low-lying areas, you know you're going to be dealing with some flooding.
And the winds will only increase as we go through tomorrow morning.
55, Del Mar at Belmar.
50 in New York City.
Over 60 in Montauk.
Boston, you'll be getting it through Sunday morning for sure, before this thing finally begins to weaken and wind down.
Rainfall will be an issue.
We will see some flooding with this, but the wind and the coastal flooding, I think, will be the main issues with this event.
All right, three hurricanes in the Pacific.
We've only had hurricanes this strong three at a time.

This is the third time in history, and Nolo has rapidly intensified now-- south of the big island, less than 200 miles away right now, and will be drifting off towards the north and then likely making a left turn, thank goodness.

But it will be intensifying as it does so, will be whipping the big island with big time, with tropical storm force winds and rain up to 25 inches, potentially more in the way of catastrophic flooding here as we head through Saturday and Sunday.
A dangerous weekend on the Pacific and here along the Atlantic Coast for sure.
Tony?
Rob, thank you.
The National Hurricane Center is warning folks on Hawaii's big island to find a safe place and stay there until well into Saturday as Hurricane Nolo passes by.
Our Carter Evans is there with the latest tonight.
Tony, we're in the community of Naalehu here on the big island.
And what you're looking at is what's left over from Hurricane Lala just a little over a month ago.
You can see that truck and home flooded out.
This building, neighbors told us, moved about 30 feet in floodwaters.
Now, take a look.
The debris field continues over here.
Here's a foundation for another home that ended up all the way across the street.
Now, with Hurricane Nolo, the forecast is about two feet of rain in some areas, and that's leading to concerns here that all of this could happen again.
Well, the red carpet at the White House is backend storage as President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping ended their summit in Washington today.
And the state of the relationship is, to be continued.
The two leaders announced they will meet two more times by the end of the year.
CBS's Weijia Jiang shows us where things stand.
We've made tremendous strides.
WEIJIA JIANG: The three-day state visit ended with a tea ceremony and a tour of the National Archives, where President Trump showed off the Declaration of Independence.
This is a great building.
WEIJIA JIANG: There was no shortage of declarations of friendship and pomp, and China announced it was sending two pandas to Atlanta this month.
But Chinese President Xi Jinping left Washington without any major deals or an agreement on AI.
Trump said she seemed to his idea of calling it "super intelligence.
That would be SUPER!
Everyone last night agreed," he posted.
As for the war on Iran, Trump did not say if he pressured Xi to cut off economic ties with Tehran, or if they talked about Taiwan.

On the domestic front, Trump scored a legal victory today in a ruling, the Supreme Court sided with the administration over the controversial use of a Social Security database to review state voter rolls, an effort to look for potential non-citizens.
The plaintiffs said in a statement, "It puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections."

New tonight, a group of bipartisan senators sent a letter to President Trump, urging him to reconsider the US invitation to Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami this December.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it an opportunity for Putin not only to engage with Trump, but other world leaders, Tony.
TONY DOKOUPIL: Weijia, thank you.
This week, the world also heard from the president of Iran, who told the United Nations General Assembly that his country would never, quote, "bend the knee," in response to American pressure.
But Iran is apparently ready to resume talks, as he told Face the Nation moderator Margaret Brennan in a network exclusive interview.
Margaret, good evening to you.
What'd you learn?
Good evening to you, Tony.

Well, President Pezeshkian survived the US-Israel bombings in Tehran, and the Trump administration granted him both a security detail and a visa to be on US soil, despite our two countries being at war.
He came with a defiant message, but also dangling a diplomatic proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
When do you expect to get a response from the United States?
INTERPRETER: If this message reaches the President of the United States or those involved in the discussions, naturally, the process will begin from the very day they accept it.
What would be the conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
INTERPRETER: We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan.

Now, in fact, there is a framework along the same path with the same objectives that were established, and ultimately the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages.
If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before.
If President Trump accepts this proposal, can you guarantee your military will abide by it?
INTERPRETER: Obviously, we will abide by whatever we commit to.
Tony, that previous agreement obviously did not hold, but Iran believes they've now ironed out some of the important details around shipping routes.

Iran's proposing to reopen the Strait after seven days, but only if the US grants them immediate sanctions relief and the ability to sell oil-- terms President Trump faced fierce criticism for within his own party when he agreed to those back in June.
Really interesting, important conversation.
Margaret, thank you.
And a note for our viewers, you can see more of that interview this Sunday on Face the Nation.
And still ahead on the broadcast tonight, what this nine-year-old girl is doing to mark Dolly Parton day today.
[DOLLY PARTON, "9 TO 5"] Working 9 to 5.
Today, of course, September 25, or 9-2-5, which is now also Dolly Parton Day.
Fans honoring not only her career, but the difference she made in the lives of others.
Mark Strassmann reports tonight from a children's hospital in Knoxville that bears her name.
Take big breaths through your mouth.
MARK STRASSMANN: Everyone had a halter meets-- Go, Tennessee.
Who are you pulling for?
MARK STRASSMANN: --feels it-- 116.1.
MARK STRASSMANN: her Dolly Parton sparkle.
She's nine now, full of life.
But at nine months, doctors here diagnosed a rare leukemia.
MELISSA HALTER: You literally get the diagnosis your daughter has cancer, and then next day you're getting the central line put in.
WEIJIA JIANG: You're such a happy kid.
Mm-mm.
MARK STRASSMANN: It's so great to see.
Yeah.
But were the times when it was hard.
I don't really remember when I was like a baby when I had cancer, but it was hard to go through it.
MARK STRASSMANN: This Knoxville facility treated Hattie years before renaming itself the Dolly Parton Children's Hospital.
It's a philanthropic collaboration with the queen of country's foundation.
RAY PAIS: Her good name rubs off on the hospital.
I think her reputation would make people trust the hospital.
(SINGING) Jolene, Jolene, Jolene MARK STRASSMANN: Hattie Halter never met her hero.
Do you feel as though you're a little Dolly?
Yes.
I definitely feel like her.
MARK STRASSMANN: And sings like her in pop-up concerts, like this.
(SINGING) It's enough to drive you crazy if you let it 9 to 5.
MARK STRASSMANN: Melissa Halter noticed its new sparkle inside, with Dolly's name now outside.
Dolly gave them a challenge.
Like, this is my name, and I need you to live up to it.
And Hattie had some great news this week.
She gets an annual blood test.
The results came back.
And, Hattie, what was the good news?
Eight years of no cancer.
Tony, it just doesn't get any better than that.
Mark, thank you.
Up next, the White Sox made the playoffs.
Is it a miracle?
The Pope weighs in.
Pope Leo's favorite team, the Chicago White Sox, clinched a spot in the playoffs yesterday, completing one of the most amazing turnarounds in sports history.
Two years ago, they just had the worst record in baseball's history.
Sometimes call it a miracle.
Do you have anything to do with that?
No comment.
TONY DOKOUPIL: That's not a denial.
And the last time the White Sox won the series in 2005, the future holy father was there in person.
Up next, on the road, Steve Hartman, with the twin brothers making good on a childhood promise.
Finally, tonight, the story of two brothers with a special bond and a shared goal.
Here's Steve Hartman on the road.
STEVE HARTMAN: Going to the ER at Chippenham Hospital in Richmond, Virginia comes with a side effect-- DR.
JASPER: I am Dr. Jasper, and I'm Dr. Jasper.
STEVE HARTMAN: -- double vision.
The other Dr. Jasper.
STEVE HARTMAN: The Jasper twins, Travan and Travis, are co-directors of the emergency department here, but their story is singular, inspirational and completely improbable.
So to be here, it's amazing, and I don't think I could have dreamed it 40 some years ago.
It's right up the road.
Back in the old neighborhood, they were some of the poorest kids on the block.
DR.
JASPER: This is where we lived.
We had no running water.
We used to go and get water from one of the parks, and we were hungry.
Right.
Hungry-- DR.
JASPER: Yeah.
--literally and hungry for success.
Because for us, that was the only way we were going to get out.
DR.
JASPER: But they didn't know the path out, until middle school.
When the twins were 12, their uncle was hospitalized.
He was an alcoholic, and his liver was failing.
The boys were scared, really needed comforting, but they say the doctor was so dismissive, basically told them their uncle was getting what he deserved.
But right then and there they made a vow.
Yeah, we talked about it out in the hallway.
In that hallway.
Yeah.
You said, we can do better than this doctor.
Yeah.
And I think we have.
STEVE HARTMAN: And so-- DR.
JASPER: Sorry.

STEVE HARTMAN: --motivated by that experience and the will of each other, they graduated high school co-valedictorians, did undergrad at Stanford, medical school at the University of Chicago, and finally-- Wow.
STEVE HARTMAN: --back to the community where they grew up to fulfill that promise they made 40 years earlier.
DR.
JASPER: So I think all of this stuff that we went through, all of the negative days, made us who we are now.
STEVE HARTMAN: Somehow, instead of being victims of their circumstances, the Jasper twins became successful because of them, turning trauma into triumph and helplessness into healing.
It was my pleasure.
STEVE HARTMAN: Steve Hartman, on the road, in Richmond, Virginia.
DR.
JASPER: That's a nice guy.
Thank you, Steve.
That's another day in America and another week.
I'm Tony Dokoupil.
For all of us here at CBS News, good night.
